climbing_route.label: Entry at the couloir base
climbing_route.notes: The line starts around 7,800 ft where the couloir splitting the northwest face meets the glacier, and finishes near 8,800 ft — roughly 1,000 ft of climbing, commonly described as eight 60 m pitches. What you actually get depends entirely on the season: late in the year it is largely snow with a few short ice steps, while early season brings thin ice over rock and genuine mixed moves. The transition from glacier to couloir is the usual place to find a moat or bergschrund, and it widens as summer goes on. Rope up on the glacier before you reach it.

climbing_route.label: Lower couloir ice steps
climbing_route.notes: A succession of ice steps broken by lower-angle snow and neve. In good conditions the steps run about 70-80 degrees with occasional bulges going near-vertical for a body length or two, and the ice can be thick enough to take screws on a single swing. In lean or late-season conditions the same ground is thin ice over rock and small passive rock gear becomes the only protection available. Parties frequently simul-climb the easier connecting snow between steps rather than pitching it out.

climbing_route.label: Upper couloir and exit
climbing_route.notes: Continued steep snow and ice to a small flat area just below the summit ridge. The couloir is a narrow, confined funnel with the whole face feeding into it, so anything the leader dislodges — dinner-plate ice, thawing rock — goes straight down onto the belay. Climb one at a time through the steeper steps where the terrain allows it, and treat afternoon warming as a hard turnaround trigger. Retreat means rappelling the couloir off ice and rock anchors, which is slow; the practical escape once you are high is to finish over the top.

climbing_route.label: Knife-edge ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: From the flat spot at the top of the couloir, gain the narrow summit ridge and follow it to the true summit. This is the mountain's well-known knife edge — a snow arete with steep drops on both sides, straightforward moving but with no margin for a slip and prone to cornicing on one side. Descent is by the standard East Ridge, not by reversing the couloir. A rack of ice screws (parties report using seven), a couple of pickets and a small selection of nuts and cams covers the route in most conditions.

climbing_route.label: West-side scree gully
climbing_route.notes: Despite the peak's steep profile from a distance, erosion has left a straightforward line up its western flank. The gully is deep loose scree with a boot path dug into it in places, and progress is the usual two-steps-up-one-back on that surface. Parties often stay in or beside a seasonal streambed low down where the footing is firmer. The main hazard here is kicking rock down onto anyone below — spread out rather than climbing in a line, and wear a helmet.

climbing_route.label: Ramp onto the upper west face
climbing_route.notes: The gully is left by a ramp trending left onto the west side proper, over mixed dirt, grass and broken rock. This exit is the one route-finding decision on the climb and parties do get drawn too high or too low before correcting; the correct ramp is the one that keeps a continuous walkable line rather than dead-ending against steeper rock.

climbing_route.label: Summit rock scramble
climbing_route.notes: The final section is enjoyable hands-on scrambling on the granodiorite and quartz diorite of the surrounding pluton, generally more solid than the scree below. Route-finding stays simple and the moves are short.

climbing_route.label: Twin summits
climbing_route.notes: The top is split into two points about 100 ft apart. The north summit is the true and marginally higher one; the south summit is a noticeably steeper inclined slab. The whole summit area is small and drops away within a few paces in most directions, and a slip off the south slab runs down the East Face — so the exposure, not the difficulty, is what deserves attention here. Several nearby lower rock points can be mistaken for the summit.

climbing_route.label: Lower face rock below the ice patch
climbing_route.notes: From the Boston Glacier, start up the rock immediately below and left of the conspicuous ice patch on the lower face. This first section runs about 300 ft and was recorded on the first ascent as grade III climbing protected with a few pitons. Getting off the glacier and onto the rock involves the usual moat or bergschrund at the margin, which grows through the season. Note that this face is climbed rarely enough that no maintained fixed gear should be assumed and modern first-hand descriptions are scarce, so treat this outline as an outline.

climbing_route.label: The ice patch
climbing_route.notes: The route's technical centrepiece: roughly 300 ft of ice at about 50 degrees. It is a north-facing feature that has thinned across the range over recent decades, so the depth of ice available for screws should be verified on the day rather than assumed. Everything on the face above funnels through this section, making it the exposed spot for rock and ice released from higher up.

climbing_route.label: Upper face to the summit
climbing_route.notes: About 600 ft remain above the ice patch. The angle is steep, but the rock is laid in upward-dipping slabs which makes the climbing easier than it looks from below. Above this the face merges into the summit. Descent is not by reversing the face — the normal descent is a high traverse below the east ridge that skirts the ridge gendarmes rather than following the crest, and it is a long committing exit in its own right; the peak has a reputation for having no easy way down by any route.

wa_frenzel_spitz_south_route.skip_reason: No published description of the climbing above the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col could be found. Available material covers only the approach into Crescent Creek Basin and the gully to the col, plus passing mentions of the peak being tagged during Southern Pickets enchainments. The peak's height, first-ascent year and general character are recorded, but nothing describes the South Route's terrain, class or hazards, and writing that section would mean inventing it.

climbing_route.label: Snowfields onto the glacier toe
climbing_route.notes: From the Boulder Basin camp at 5,500-6,000 ft, head southeast up snowfields and moraine to gain the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. This is the one place parties routinely go wrong: taking the left-hand moraine commits you to an awkward traverse beneath a wall of loose rock and then across a steep snowfield to recover the correct line. Sort the entry out in daylight if you can, and rope up before stepping onto glacier ice.

climbing_route.label: Lower glacier corridor
climbing_route.notes: Trend slightly south to take the corridor on the left side of the rock feature that divides the lower glacier, then work back northeast. Both open and hidden crevasses are present here and the crossing points shift year to year and even week to week, so expect to weave and to reverse a line or two. Late-season melt-out exposes more bare ice and pushes the practical route further off any recorded track — a GPS trace from a previous party is a hint, not a route.

climbing_route.label: Upper glacier to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: Continue northeast up the upper glacier to a saddle at roughly 9,500 ft just east of Sitkum Spire. The firn line on the upper glacier has been retreating and bare ice is increasingly exposed, which makes crampons and a firmer belay standard rather than optional in late summer. A bergschrund sits below the saddle and is the last crevasse hazard on the ascent. This is a shaded, exposed slope late in the day — softening snow after mid-morning is the reason parties leave camp in the small hours.

climbing_route.label: Sitkum Ridge pumice
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, leave the glacier for the pumice of Sitkum Ridge. This is loose, ball-bearing volcanic debris on a moderate slope — no technical difficulty, but tiring underfoot and easy to send rock down onto anyone behind. Most parties unrope here. Being off the glacier, it is also the point where a whiteout descent becomes hard to navigate by feel, so mark the spot where you leave the snow.

climbing_route.label: Summit slope
climbing_route.notes: Stay to the right of and slightly below the summit as you gain height, then take the snow chute that leads up to the top. The whole route is a glacier and snow climb with no rock pitches, but it is a long day at altitude on an isolated volcano where weather closes in quickly and the descent retraces every crevasse crossing made on the way up.

wa_golden_horn_north_face.skip_reason: Only the fact of the 1958 north face ascent is on record; no pitch, terrain, grade or hazard description of that line could be found in any accessible source. Published route material for this peak covers the southwest scramble and, separately, a modern east face line — neither describes the north face. Reports do note the peak's rock ranges from good bands to very loose ground, but that is general and not specific to this route, so nothing here can be written honestly.

climbing_route.label: Talus fan below the south face
climbing_route.notes: Ascend the fan of large talus blocks that runs up to the base of the south face directly below the summit. The blocks are big enough to walk on but some shift; the cairns that mark the way lower down have usually thinned to nothing by here, so the line is chosen by eye toward the base of the ramp above.

climbing_route.label: The hidden ramp
climbing_route.notes: The route's crux, and it is short. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and is not obvious until you are underneath it. The hard part is the single step off the boulder at its foot: the left-hand option passes a chockstone and involves a steep low fifth-class move, while the right-hand option is a steep, exposed Class 3-4 sequence on solid holds and is the line most parties take. Above that step the ramp itself eases. Some parties sling the ramp for a belay or a handline; a short rope is worth carrying even though a confident scrambler will not need it.

climbing_route.label: Upper south face to the high notch
climbing_route.notes: Above the ramp, cross the upper south face — typically over two remnant snow patches that persist well into summer — and scramble to the high notch between the west and east summits. In June, or any heavy snow year, these patches are steep snow immediately above the very exposed north side and turn a scramble into a climb needing axe and crampons; by August they are usually melted out and the section is unremarkable. Judge this from the notch below, not from the trailhead.

climbing_route.label: North-side ledge and summit block
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, traverse north-side heather ledges — easy walking, but with substantial drop below, and parties sometimes leave a handline here for the return. A short Class 3 scramble on the prominent summit block finishes the climb. The descent reverses everything, and the step down off the hidden ramp feels harder than it did going up; plan on downclimbing it carefully or rappelling from a slung block.

climbing_route.label: South side of the summit block
climbing_route.notes: The talus slope tops out on the south side of the summit block. Do not try to climb the rock straight above you here — the direct south side is steeper and more broken than it looks, and it is the spot where parties commit to the wrong line. Instead line yourself up with the south side of the block and prepare to traverse.

climbing_route.label: Traverse east under the block
climbing_route.notes: Work right, staying along the south side of the rock and heading east, until a reasonable gully opens on the east side. The traverse is on loose talus and scree over a sloping bed — the most slip-prone ground on the route, where deliberate foot placement matters more than speed. It is also the last place to turn around easily.

climbing_route.label: East gully and summit notch
climbing_route.notes: Ascend the gully on the east side of the block. It stays easy until the top, where a short notch or narrow chimney runs up to the summit rock and gives a bit of genuine Class 3 scrambling. The rock here is reported as good and the holds solid, but the position is exposed and the summit itself is a small platform with steep ground on several sides. The downclimb of this last step is the part to think about before committing to it, and wet or icy rock changes the character of the notch entirely.
